blocks.text: It is proved that קפוד kippod is the hedgehog and the porcupine.

Three elements contend over the animal קפוד kippod: some assign it to the earth, others to the water, others to the air along with the birds. In the first rank I place the Greeks and Jerome, for whom קפוד kippod is ἐχῖνος [echinos], the hedgehog, namely the land hedgehog, which lives in hedges in summer and in winter in tree trunks or in holes in the ground. Others infer that it is an aquatic animal from Esa. XIV, 23., on Babylon: I will make it a hereditary possession of the kippod and pools of water. But the ranks of these are divided in two, or even in three. Some hold it to be the tortoise, some the beaver, some the otter. All rely on the etymology of the word. For in Esa. XXXVIII, 12. קפד means to cut off, where the weaver cuts off the warp when the whole web has been woven. And these animals have a remarkable power of cutting. With the beaver the matter is very well known. It is an animal with a fearsome bite (says Pliny, book 8, chapter 30); it cuts down trees by rivers as if with iron. But Varro too, in book 4 On the Latin Language, would have the otter [lutra] named from λύειν [lyein], because it is said to undercut the roots of trees on the bank and to loosen them. The same power in the tortoise is all the more remarkable because, though it has no teeth, it nevertheless crushes everything with the edge of its beak. That is, the edges of the beak are sharp, the upper part closing over the lower in the manner of a box. So Pliny, book 11, ch. 37, and book 9, ch. 10. Similar to this is what is read of the sea turtle in Porta coeli, fol. [col. 1036] 34a: ויש לה כח גדול בפיה ובשיניה ואם תקח אבן בפיה תשבור אותה בחוק גדול לחלקים קטנים, It has enormous strength in its mouth and teeth. And if it takes a stone into its mouth, it crushes it with great force into the tiniest pieces. Add to this that in Arabic, if both Kimchis are to be believed, the name of the tortoise is קנפאר, which does not differ much from the Hebrew קפוד. But those who hold the third opinion, namely that קפוד kippod is a species of bird, object that elsewhere kippod is named by Isaiah and Zephaniah together with birds. The passage of Isaiah, chapter 34, verse 11, reads thus: The pelican and the kippod shall possess it. And Zephaniah, chapter 2, verse 14, not very differently: Both the pelican and the kippod shall lodge on its lintels. Again, these are in doubt as to what kind of bird kippod is: some explain it as the owl; others as the vulture; others as the blackbird; others as the bittern, or starry heron; others as the cypselus, which is also the apus; others as the plancus, or duck-eagle[?]; and what not? And the most learned Fuller, in his Miscellanea, book 1, chapter 18, compares most of those interpretations with one another in such a way that he rejects none except the one which alone is true. I mean that most ancient one, by which קפוד kippod is explained as the hedgehog; and many things serve to confirm it.
